scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Dinka are Nilotic peoples who have inhabited the Nile basin for centuries, maintaining an agro-pastoral lifestyle.
Their music and dance traditions are part of a broader Nilotic complex shared with the Nuer and Maasai, characterized by a focus on cattle-related symbolism and physical endurance.
Historically, these dances have served to celebrate warriors returning from conflict, mark the passage of age sets, and facilitate courtship in a society where cattle are the primary dowry.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed for rites of passage, marriage, and funerals.
It serves to 'inculcate social patterns and values' and reinforce community structures such as kinship and age status.
In a courtship context, the jumping acts as a competitive display of a man's vitality.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by high vertical leaps performed by men and circular movement by women.
Men jump from a stationary or slightly rhythmic standing position, aiming for maximum height while keeping the torso relatively stable.
Women often move in a circle around the jumpers or in a separate line, raising their arms to mimic cattle horns.
Watch for The Horn Gesture, The Vertical Leap.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Dinka music is primarily pentatonic and features prominent polyrhythms.
While the sources note that many Sudanese traditions use percussion and singing, the Dinka specifically utilize group chants and rhythmic clapping.
Listen for the Drums, Human voice (chanting), Handclapping.
The pulse is Polyrhythmic.

A dense layer of polyrhythmic drumming and handclaps supporting a pentatonic vocal melody. The sound is communal and driving, lacking the complex string harmonies of West Africa but emphasizing rhythmic entrainment.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dances take place in open communal spaces within Dinka settlements in the Bahr el Ghazal and Upper Nile regions.
While specific modern attire varies, traditional contexts involve the use of beads and skins.
The setting is often outdoors, integrated into the daily environment of the cattle camps or villages.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The sources do not name individual Dinka dancers, but note that 'master dancers and drummers' are responsible for teaching the youth to perform the movements exactly as passed down through generations.

The Dinka are spread across several regions including Jonglei and southern Kordufan; while the core jumping mechanic is consistent, local linguistic communities (among the 133 in Sudan) may introduce specific song variations or rhythmic nuances.
The dance belongs to the Nilotic family of traditions, sharing traits with the Nuer and Maasai.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Dinka jumping dance is sibling of Adumu: The Maasai jumping dance shares the Nilotic emphasis on verticality and warrior prowess.
Dinka jumping dance is variant of Dudu: A Luo dance used during beer parties, sharing the functional Nilotic roots.

narration: Step 1: Stand with feet hip-width apart, weight on the balls of the feet.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
